meta.title: The D Form, and the Chord Everywhere at Once
meta.summary: The D form is the only one whose top note is the third, and every overlap between neighbouring windows turns out to hold a complete triad of its own.

. You already know it's never played whole; now you can see what "whole" even means here. The open D chord this form comes from mutes the bottom two strings, and moving it up the neck changes nothing about that — four strings is the entire shape, not a fragment of a bigger one.

spans.text: Every overlap between two neighbouring windows holds a complete
— the strongest fact this chapter has, and one chapter 1 could only assert in roots. Here it is in chord tones.
Two of those overlaps are three adjacent strings, so they're directly playable little triads in their own right. Strings 4-3-2, all at fret
— and that isn't one form's property, it's the middle of the A form's grip
the middle of the G form's grip at once, the same three notes claimed by two forms. Strings 5-4-3, at frets
, sitting exactly where the E and D windows meet.

Wherever you stop on this neck, the notes under your hand belong to two windows at once, and there is always a whole chord sitting there. Chapter 1 could only claim the neck was continuous; here the chord tones prove it.
How to actually move between forms — sliding a progression up the neck through these overlaps — is its own chapter, later in this pathway.
The same five windows carry every layer this pathway adds. Next, two more notes go into each one — the major pentatonic. The windows never change; only how much of each one is lit.
